title: Wi-Fi CERTIFIED®: Future-proofing enterprise networks
content:
Wi-Fi® is the backbone of enterprise connectivity. From office complexes to sprawling campuses and hospitals, Wi-Fi fuels the mission-critical applications that keep businesses running. But today’s enterprise is evolving faster than ever before — and so are its connectivity requirements. As the pace of digital transformation accelerates, enterprises are facing new challenges that require more sophisticated, secure, and scalable Wi-Fi solutions.
Wi-Fi enables a new era of enterprise networking
The growing demand for cloud-based services, distributed workforces, and connected devices is putting new pressures on enterprise networks. With a projected 20% compound annual growth rate in enterprise networking equipment and more than 747 million shipments expected by 2027,
[1]
enterprise networks must deliver increased performance and security
.
Several powerful trends are reshaping connectivity in the enterprise landscape:
Reliance on the cloud
: with workloads moving to the cloud, enterprise networks must support faster, more reliable data transmission as even minor lags can disrupt business operations or halt production lines
Remote and distributed workforces
: today’s employees connect from home offices, satellite branches, or on the go, often using bandwidth-intensive apps like video conferencing and augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR)
Proliferation of devices
: today’s enterprise supports a vast array of endpoints, including laptops, smartphones, security cameras, IoT sensors, and even medical equipment, each with unique connectivity needs
Security at the forefront
: cyberattacks are becoming more frequent and more costly, with the average breach now topping $4.88 million.
[2]
As “bring your own device” (BYOD) and Internet of Things (IoT) adoption continues to grow, network security must evolve to protect both legacy and modern devices
Complex device lifecycles
: while Wi-Fi infrastructure may refresh every 3-5 years, many devices, particularly in healthcare settings, may remain in service for as long as 15 years. It is critical that enterprise networks are able to balance performance and backward compatibility for the long haul
Enterprise connectivity challenges
Wi-Fi equipment makers, service providers, and systems integrators face a host of unique challenges as they design and deploy solutions for enterprise environments. Today’s enterprise networks must support:
Interoperability:
due to an increasingly varied array of endpoint devices across multiple vendors
Backward compatibility:
networks must connect devices with multiple generations of Wi-Fi
Security:
devices and networks must be equipped to protect an organization and its customers against cyberattacks
Performance:
low latency is essential for many business-critical applications as even brief delays can affect productivity — a challenge that will only intensify as more enterprises implement AI applications
Minimal network congestion:
enterprise networks are uniquely dense due in part to a large volume of users and high peak upload and download traffic
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED drives enterprise success
In Wi-Fi’s 25 year history,
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED®
has played an essential role in accelerating the technology’s adoption by helping to ensure reliability, security, and interoperability among Wi-Fi devices. As connectivity needs continue to evolve, Wi-Fi CERTIFIED  delivers the high-performance, scalable  solutions enterprise demands.
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED 6® & Wi-Fi CERTIFIED 7™:
the latest Wi-Fi generations operate in the 2.4 GHz, 5 GHz, and 6 GHz bands to support high bandwidth, low latency applications in dense environments
Wi-Fi QoS Management™:
allows enterprise networks to prioritize traffic flows for time-sensitive services like video and telepresence
WPA3™:
provides cutting-edge security protocols to safeguard data and protect against threats
Wi-Fi Enhanced Open™:
preserves the convenience of open networks while minimizing risk
Wi-Fi Location™:
delivers accurate location information to enable indoor navigation and asset tracking
Passpoint®:
enables streamlined authentication for seamless connectivity between Wi-Fi networks and mobile devices
Wi-Fi Device Metrics:
provides a framework for device performance across diverse use cases to help IT managers and network architects better evaluate client devices for a superior experience
Discover the full potential of Wi-Fi in enterprise
Enterprise networks are only as strong as the technology behind them. As the connectivity landscape continues to evolve, Wi-Fi Alliance® will continue to drive technology advancements and solutions that ensure Wi-Fi remains the first choice for enterprise.
Download the brochure
to learn more about how Wi-Fi CERTIFIED provides the secure, reliable, and scalable foundation for enterprise connectivity.

title: Powering a connected world: Wi-Fi® momentum in 2025
content:
A leader in connectivity
Wi-Fi® remains a fundamental component of wireless connectivity. 3.9 billion Wi-Fi devices are expected to ship in 2025, bringing total Wi-Fi shipments to 48.8 billion over the technology’s lifetime.
[1]
Currently, 23.3 billion Wi-Fi devices are in use,
[2]
found in homes with security cameras and voice assistants, enterprises with wireless printers and video conferencing systems, and industrial settings with automated machinery and sensors. Both inside and outside the home, users spend 77 - 88% of their screen-on time connected to Wi-Fi while using a smartphone,
[3]
underscoring Wi-Fi’s significance in daily life.
6 GHz Wi-Fi: Enhancing capabilities
The adoption of 6 GHz unlicensed spectrum for Wi-Fi has improved the technology’s performance, offering higher data rates, lower latency, and better reliability. Utilized by Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7, this additional spectrum supports applications like extended reality (XR), ultra-high definition video streaming, and Industrial Internet of Things (IIoT). As of 2025, 12 countries have unlocked the entire 6 GHz band for Wi-Fi use, enabling broader access to these cutting-edge use cases. 6 GHz devices have gained traction, with 583.2 million Wi-Fi 7 devices and 626.9 million Wi-Fi 6E devices projected to ship this year.
[4]
Over 2,000 6 GHz devices have achieved Wi-Fi CERTIFIED® status, up 22% from the end of last year, indicating market demand for certified Wi-Fi products.
Growth across sectors
Wi-Fi’s significance is evident across various industries, based on 2025 shipment forecasts:
Networking:
81.6 million Wi-Fi 6E access points (APs) and 98.7 million Wi-Fi 7 APs are expected to ship, strengthening network infrastructure
[5]
Automotive:
97.5 million Wi-Fi products will support vehicle systems, including diagnostics and over-the-air (OTA) updates
[6]
Healthcare:
76.4 million Wi-Fi devices will be used in areas like telemedicine and medical equipment
[7]
IoT:
1.6 billion Wi-Fi IoT devices will ship, contributing to connected homes, cities, and industries
[8]
These numbers indicate Wi-Fi’s steady integration into multiple market segments. Beyond shipments, Wi-Fi is projected to contribute $4.9 trillion USD to the global economy in 2025,
[9]
highlighting its broader economic significance.
Reflecting on strong progress
Wi-Fi has remained relevant by continuously evolving its standards and testing processes to meet changing technology needs. Efforts like Wi-Fi CERTIFIED ensure devices meet performance and interoperability benchmarks, supporting a high-quality, reliable user experience. The technology’s ability to adapt to varying network demands — whether in dense urban areas or remote locations — contributes to its overall value. As connectivity needs shift, Wi-Fi’s ongoing enhancements position it to handle future challenges and support new opportunities.

title: Powering progress: 6 GHz Wi-Fi® delivers a connected future

Wi-Fi Stakeholders Letter to the U.S. Congressional Committees
content:
Dear Chairman Cruz, Ranking Member Cantwell, Chairman Guthrie, and Ranking Member Pallone:
On behalf of the diverse ecosystem of American technology companies and associations that rely on Wi-Fi connectivity, we write to update the committees on the United States’ successful use of the 6 GHz band since it was designated for unlicensed use under the first Trump Administration. American companies are leading Wi-Fi development and helping to ensure United States’ leadership in international competitiveness, fostering innovation, and driving economic growth. The 6 GHz band constitutes the foundation for Wi-Fi’s continued development and growth, because the band’s characteristics are perfectly suited to indoor networking that is the hallmark of Wi-Fi, while being flexible enough to support targeted outdoor uses. In locations ranging from small businesses and homes to stadiums, hospitals, schools, wearables, and advanced manufacturing, Wi-Fi is the workhorse of the internet.
Read full letter

title: Wi-Fi Stakeholders Letter to the U.S. Congressional Committees [PDF]
content:
June 2, 2025   The Honorable Ted Cruz    The Honorable Maria Cantwell Chairman      Ranking Member U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce,  U.S. Senate Committee on Commerce,     Science, and Transportation       Science, and Transportation Washington, DC 20510    Washington, DC 20510   The Honorable Brett Guthrie     The Honorable Frank Pallone, Jr. Chairman      Ranking Member U.S. House Committee on Energy and  U.S. House Committee on Energy and    Commerce         Commerce 2125 Rayburn House Office Building  2322A Rayburn House Office Building Washington, DC 20515    Washington, DC 20515   Dear Chairman Cruz, Ranking Member Cantwell, Chairman Guthrie, and Ranking Member Pallone:   On behalf of the diverse ecosystem of American technology companies and associations that rely on Wi-Fi connectivity, we write to update the committees on the United States’ successful use of the 6 GHz band since it was designated for unlicensed use under the first Trump Administration. American companies are leading Wi-Fi development and helping to ensure United States’ leadership in international competitiveness, fostering innovation, and driving economic growth. The 6 GHz band constitutes the foundation for Wi-Fi’s continued development and growth, because the band’s characteristics are perfectly suited to indoor networking that is the hallmark of Wi-Fi, while being flexible enough to support targeted outdoor uses.  In locations ranging from small businesses and homes to stadiums, hospitals, schools, wearables, and advanced manufacturing, Wi-Fi is the workhorse of the internet.    Since the Federal Communications Commission opened the 6 GHz band for unlicensed use during President Trump’s first term,1 enterprises and consumers have been using the band for a wide range of purposes. Shipments of 6 GHz-enabled consumer devices in North America,  1 Unlicensed Use of the 6 GHz Band; Expanding Flexible Use in Mid-Band Spectrum Between 3.7 and 24 GHz, Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, 33 FCC Rcd 10496, 10499-501, paras. 8-13 (2018) (Notice); Unlicensed Use of the 6 GHz Band; Expanding Flexible Use in Mid-Band Spectrum Between 3.7 and 24 GHz, Report and Order and Further Notice of Proposed Rulemaking, 35 FCC Rcd 3852, 3855, para. 7 (2020) (6 GHz Order), reversed in part, aff’d in part and remanded, AT&T Servs. Inc., v. FCC, 21 F.4th 841, 853-54 (D.C. Cir. 2020) (affirming 6 GHz Order and reversing and remanding to address issue of whether to “reserve a sliver of the 6 GHz band for licensed mobile operation”).  The 2020 decision opened 6 GHz spectrum to use by Low Power Indoor devices and set the regulatory framework for Standard Power Devices operating pursuant to an Automated Frequency Coordination system, an innovation ultimately approved for commercial use in 2022. OET Announces Conditional Approval for 6 GHz Band Automated Frequency Coordination Systems, Public Notice, 37 FCC Rcd (2022). A subsequent 2024 order added rules that enable Very Low Power devices to operate throughout the band. Unlicensed Use of the 6 GHz Band; Expanding Flexible Use in Mid-Band Spectrum Between 3.7 and 24 GHz, Third Report and Order (rel. Dec.13, 2024).  
 2 
totaling 95 million last year, are expected to reach nearly 370 million per year by 2029.2 Businesses across industries have leveraged the enhanced performance of the latest Wi-Fi standards to improve operations, increase productivity, and deliver better services. From hospitals deploying high-density wireless networks to support telemedicine, to factories leveraging robotics and IoT devices for precision work and data-gathering, to schools and libraries deploying Wi-Fi to improve educational experiences, as well as the advanced provision of broadband services broadly throughout the United States by providers in rural areas deploying both Wi-Fi and other broadband technologies, the 6 GHz band has become a critical enabler of innovation. Consumers have benefited from 6 GHz unlicensed broadband connections in rural and other underserved areas, and throughout the U.S. via in-home Wi-Fi networks that make the most of the speed and performance of increasingly fast broadband connections. Indeed, by 2030, most U.S. households will be served by 6 GHz access points utilizing channels as large as 320 megahertz.3 These deployments demonstrate not only robust demand for improved and more capable Wi-Fi, but also Wi-Fi’s ability to coexist successfully with incumbent users, preserving critical operations while unlocking new opportunities.   Wi-Fi is a vital driver of America’s economic strength. A recent study estimates that Wi-Fi technologies, including unlicensed 6 GHz operations, contribute significantly to the U.S. economy, such that by 2027, the annual economic value of Wi-Fi is projected to reach $2.4 trillion, including an estimated $514 billion in consumer benefit, $624 billion in producer surplus, and $1,286 billion in GDP contribution.4  Wi-Fi is also projected to support more than 13 million jobs by 2027 and approximately 21 million jobs by 2032, with 6 GHz operations specifically contributing to more than half of those positions.5 This impact is expected to grow exponentially as new applications and industries adopt next-generation technologies powered by the band. Retaining this spectrum for unlicensed use will continue to generate substantial economic value while reinforcing the United States as a global leader in connectivity and technology development.  Looking ahead, the 6 GHz band will play a pivotal role in enabling the technologies of the next decade, including artificial intelligence (AI), advanced manufacturing, augmented and virtual reality, and other groundbreaking innovations. AI-driven systems, for example, require robust, high-capacity wireless networks to process and transmit massive amounts of data in real time. Similarly, the future of manufacturing relies on smart factories powered by reliable, low-latency wireless connections to optimize efficiency and reduce costs. The 6 GHz band provides the critical infrastructure needed to support these advancements, ensuring that the United States remains at the forefront of technological progress. Unlicensed spectrum is the foundation for all of these advances as it enables permissionless innovation, unlocking the potential of  2 See Andrew Spivey, ABIresearch, “Wi-Fi Innovation and Future Spectrum Allocation,” at 4 (2024), https://go.abiresearch.com/hubfs/Marketing/Whitepapers/Wi-Fi%20Innovation%20and%20Future%20Spectrum%20Allocation/ABI_Research%20Wi-Fi%20Innovation%20and%20Future%20Spectrum%20Allocation.pdf?hsCtaAttrib=183432523558. 3 Id. at 8. 4 Telecom Advisory Services, “Wi-Fi Works: How the Success of Wi-Fi Drives U.S. Job Creation,” at 5 (Apr. 2025), https://wififorward.org/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Wi-Fi-and-employment_3.25.25-v259.pdf.  5 Id. at 4. 
 3

title: 6 GHz Wi-Fi®: 5 years of unparalleled wireless innovation
content:
Five years ago, the Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC)
landmark decision
to make Wi-Fi® available to 6 GHz spectrum opened the door to unprecedented innovation and unlocked billions of dollars in economic value. To commemorate this important milestone, we spoke with Alex Roytblat, Vice President of Worldwide Regulatory Affairs at Wi-Fi Alliance®, for more insight on how 6 GHz Wi-Fi catalyzed advancements in wireless connectivity and what’s ahead for the future.
As we reflect on the past five years, what do you see as the most significant development for Wi-Fi in the 6 GHz band?
Over the past five years, the most significant development for Wi-Fi in the 6 GHz band has been the global regulatory momentum to open this spectrum for unlicensed use, starting with the FCC’s landmark decision in April 2020. That decision catalyzed a
wave of similar regulatory actions in other countries
, allowing 6 GHz Wi-Fi technology to develop and deliver multigigabit, low-latency connectivity on a scale never before possible. In parallel, the rapid integration of 6 GHz Wi-Fi radios into devices – from smartphones and laptops to enterprise-grade APs – demonstrates strong industry alignment and validates the commercial viability of 6 GHz Wi-Fi. This combination of regulatory progress and ecosystem readiness has fundamentally redefined what's possible for Wi-Fi, especially in high-density and performance-critical environments.
What do you think is the most underrated innovation to come out of opening the 6 GHz band to Wi-Fi? What's the most overhyped?
The most underrated innovation from opening the 6 GHz band to Wi-Fi is the enablement of deterministic, low-latency performance in dense environments – especially through the broader adoption of
Wi-Fi 7's scheduling and multi-link capabilities
. These advanced features are quietly transforming Wi-Fi from a best-effort technology into a serious contender for real-time, high-reliability applications like augmented and virtual reality (AR/VR), industrial automation, and telemedicine.
The most overhyped aspect is the narrative that 6 GHz Wi-Fi alone will instantly revolutionize user experiences. While the spectrum is critical, its benefits are only fully realized with corresponding ecosystem advancements – such as support in client devices, upgrades to infrastructure, and deployment in environments that actually need the extra bandwidth. Without those pieces in place, the raw spectrum alone doesn't solve congestion or deliver gigabit speeds by default.
What are some of the biggest opportunities for developers and device makers as 6 GHz Wi-Fi becomes more widespread?
As 6 GHz Wi-Fi becomes more widespread, developers and device makers are positioned to unlock entirely new classes of user experiences. With access to wider channels and lower interference, there’s room to design for real-time, high-bandwidth applications – think untethered AR/VR, cloud gaming, 8K streaming, and AI-powered assistants that rely on rapid edge-to-cloud interactions.
For developers, this means pushing the envelope on apps that demand consistent low latency and high throughput, especially in education, healthcare, industrial IoT, and immersive media. There's also an opportunity to optimize multi-link operation and adaptive connectivity strategies that take full advantage of 6 GHz performance.
For device makers, the ability to differentiate with next-generation Wi-Fi performance – whether through better thermal design, antenna systems, or software optimization – creates a competitive advantage. And as
Automated Frequency Coordination (AFC) enables outdoor use
, we’ll also see growth in W-Fi devices tailored for smart cities, outdoor mesh networks, and rural broadband.
Not all countries have made the 6 GHz band available to Wi-Fi. What is the impact on users in countries where the full 6 GHz band is not available?
In countries where the full 6 GHz band isn’t available to Wi-Fi, users are at a significant disadvantage, both in terms of performance and access to innovation. Devices may technically support advanced features like Wi-Fi 6E or Wi-Fi 7, but without the full band, they can’t deliver the wide 160 or 320 MHz channels that enable multi-gigabit speeds and ultra-low latency. This impacts everything from everyday connectivity – like streaming, gaming, and video conferencing – to more transformational use cases such as AR/VR or edge-AI solutions in education, telemedicine, and smart manufacturing. In short, users are stuck with congested legacy bands while others are moving into a new era of wireless connectivity. Moreover, the global tech ecosystem is rapidly standardizing around 6 GHz Wi-Fi. When a country lags in spectrum availability, it risks creating a digital divide – not just internally, but in terms of international competitiveness, access to next-gen applications, and alignment with global supply chains. The opportunity cost of delay is real and growing.
Looking towards the future of wireless connectivity, how do you think 6 GHz Wi-Fi will continue to fuel innovation? What are some of the most impactful advancements you foresee in the next few years?
Looking ahead, 6 GHz Wi-Fi will be a foundational enabler for the next wave of innovation across multiple sectors. With the clean, wide channels it provides, we’ll see continued growth in high-throughput, low-latency applications, especially immersive technologies like AR/VR/XR, real-time collaboration tools, and AI-driven edge computing.
One of the most impactful advancements will be the broader deployment of Wi-Fi 7, which leverages features like Multi-link Operation (MLO), 320 MHz channels, and deterministic latency to unlock use cases that were previously out of reach for Wi-Fi. This will make wireless truly viable for mission-critical enterprise, healthcare, and industrial environments. On the infrastructure side, AFC will open the door for standard power outdoor Wi-Fi, dramatically expanding coverage and enabling fiber-like performance in suburban and rural areas, helping to bridge the digital divide with lower-cost solutions. In short, 6 GHz Wi-Fi isn’t just keeping pace with innovation – it’s setting the stage for it.

Alex Roytblat is Vice President of Worldwide Regulatory Affairs, where he is responsible for managing and overseeing all regulatory matters and compliance issues related to the Wi-Fi ecosystem. In his role, Alex works with Wi-Fi Alliance members, directors and executives to advance policy priorities with policymakers, regulators and other stakeholders.
With more than 25 years of experience in telecom regulations, Alex is an internationally recognized expert with a deep understanding of the regulatory landscape. Prior to joining Wi-Fi Alliance, Alex served at the United States Federal Communications Commission, where he was involved in all phases of domestic and international radio spectrum management processes. Previously, Alex held technical roles at Stanford Telecommunications and Booz Allen & Hamilton. title: Wi-Fi Alliance® welcomes introduction of budget reconciliation text
content:
Austin, TX and Washington, D.C. – May 12, 2025 –
Wi-Fi Alliance® commends Chairman Brett Guthrie and the House Committee on Energy and Commerce for introducing the budget reconciliation text. This legislative initiative represents a positive step toward strengthening the United States’ communications infrastructure and ensuring continued spectrum innovation.
We are especially encouraged that the bill explicitly excludes the 5.925–7.125 GHz frequency range. This provision is vital to preserving unlicensed access to the entire 6 GHz band — a foundational resource for the future of Wi-Fi technology.  By providing much-needed regulatory clarity, the bill encourages continued investment and innovation in next-generation Wi-Fi technologies, which are already delivering transformative benefits to consumers, enterprises, and public institutions.
The Communications Subtitle of the bill reaffirms Congress's recognition of the central role unlicensed spectrum plays in powering connectivity, enabling economic growth, and supporting key national priorities such as education, telehealth, and small business competitiveness.
Wi-Fi Alliance looks forward to continued collaboration with policymakers to ensure that U.S. spectrum policy keeps pace with the evolving demands of a wireless-first world.
For more information, visit:
energycommerce.house.gov

title: Episode 80: The ISP evolution and prioritizing more efficient Wi-Fi® with Metin Taskin of Airties

In today's episode, we welcome Metin Taskin, Founder and CEO of Airties, back to the podcast to talk about how Internet Service Providers are rethinking the way they deliver and manage in-home Wi-Fi. Metin tells us that user experience is becoming the new battleground for customer loyalty, and we learn that standards like Wi-Fi EasyMesh are enabling more consistent service. We also talk about why technologies like Wi-Fi 7 and 5G FWA are pushing operators to invest in smarter, more adaptive networks, and Metin shares his insight about how ISPs are using automation, data, and new testing tools to stay ahead. title: Wi-Fi Alliance® commemorates landmark 6 GHz decision
content:
Transformational spectrum decision catalyzed unprecedented innovation and connectivity advancements
Austin, Texas – April 23, 2025
– Wi-Fi Alliance® proudly marks the fifth anniversary of the U.S. Federal Communications Commission’s (FCC)
landmark decision
to open the 6 GHz band for unlicensed use, a pivotal milestone that continues to fuel innovation and connectivity through Wi-Fi®. This bold April 2020 decision unlocked billions of dollars in economic value, positioned the U.S. as a global leader in unlicensed spectrum policy, and catalyzed international momentum toward enabling a next-generation Wi-Fi® ecosystem worldwide.
The 6 GHz band has played a critical role in enabling next-generation Wi-Fi – driving the global rollout of Wi-Fi 7 – by relieving network congestion and expanding high-performance connectivity. Since the FCC’s ruling, billions of 6 GHz Wi-Fi devices have entered the market, underscoring the rapid adoption and far-reaching benefits of forward-looking spectrum policy.
"The FCC’s visionary action to open the full 6 GHz band was a pivotal moment for Wi-Fi connectivity and digital transformation globally," said Kevin Robinson, President and CEO of Wi-Fi Alliance. "Five years on, that leadership continues to drive global spectrum policy, as regulators around the world empower consumers and enterprises with Wi-Fi innovation.”
Wi-Fi Alliance is proud of the critical role we've played at the forefront of advancing 6 GHz Wi-Fi, working tirelessly to support policymakers and industry innovators. As we look ahead, we remain committed to driving further progress in spectrum policy and fostering global connectivity through continued leadership in Wi-Fi advancements.
To mark this milestone, Wi-Fi Alliance is sharing
educational resources
, a
special episode
of The Signal podcast, and member company testimonials on the tremendous impact of the full band.
As the demand for high-quality connectivity continues to grow, 6 GHz remains essential to delivering seamless, secure, and scalable Wi-Fi.
Wi-Fi Alliance member testimonials
“The 6 GHz band for unlicensed use is advancing the wireless landscape, and Boingo is pioneering its real-world deployment across high-density venues with our Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7 solutions. From airports and stadiums to hospitals, convention centers and military bases, Boingo helps venues unlock the full potential of the 6 GHz band to deliver faster speeds, greater capacity, and seamless, secure connected experiences—all through our converged network approach.” – Dr. Derek Peterson, CTO,
Boingo Wireless
“Five years ago, the FCC’s bold move to open the 6 GHz band didn’t just transform U.S. wireless connectivity—it set a global precedent. Today, countries representing over 75% of the world’s GDP have followed suit, catalyzing a new era of Wi-Fi innovation. With over a billion 6 GHz Wi-Fi devices shipped, it’s quickly becoming the standard for smartphones and laptops. As Wi-Fi 7 proliferates, wireless performance is converging with AI—powering an immersive, intelligent edge. The momentum behind 6 GHz is unstoppable, and the next chapter of Wi-Fi is redefining how we connect, compute, and collaborate.” – Vijay Nagarajan, Vice President of Wireless Communications and Connectivity Division,
Broadcom Inc.
“The FCC’s decision to open the 6 GHz band removed the last performance barrier for the industry. We quickly integrated 6 GHz into the Calix Unlimited Subscriber systems portfolio, building a Wi-Fi CERTIFIED® line so providers can support higher performance and capacity applications for residential, MDUs, and small businesses. The 6 GHz spectrum and the latest Wi-Fi 7 standard are game changers for providers who compete on experience, enabling remote healthcare, smart manufacturing, real-time logistics, and much more. As a contributing member of Wi-Fi Alliance, Calix remains committed to open standards that ensure interoperability and help providers deliver secure, high-performance Wi-Fi 7 experiences at scale." – Shane Eleniak, chief product officer at
Calix
"As we celebrate the 5-year anniversary of the FCC's release of the full 6 GHz band for unlicensed use, Cisco acknowledges its transformative impact on wireless connectivity. The availability of 1200 MHz in the 6 GHz spectrum has been vital for advancing network solutions and fostering innovation. Cisco will continue to build innovative technologies that are 6 GHz enabled, reflecting our commitment to connecting the unconnected and driving a digital future for all." – Matt MacPherson, Wireless CTO at
Cisco
“Wi-Fi has become ingrained in our daily lives as the predominant and most ubiquitous wireless technology over the last 26 years. The 6 GHz decision five years ago wasn’t just a regulatory milestone—it marked the beginning of what I call the era of 6 GHz Wi-Fi connectivity and mobility. This newly available spectrum has unlocked unprecedented possibilities and will continue to drive the next wave of wireless innovation. As we celebrate this anniversary, we’re reminded that the real potential of 6 GHz is just starting to unfold. At Extreme, we’re harnessing this spectrum to deliver breakthrough performance—ultra-fast, ultra-reliable connectivity that enables seamless, secure, and high-quality user experiences in even the most demanding environments. For our customers, 6 GHz Wi-Fi isn’t just an upgrade—it’s a promise of fast, frictionless, and dependable wireless access, wherever and whenever it’s needed.” –
David Coleman, Director of Wireless Networking, Office of the CTO,
Extreme Networks
“Congratulations to the FCC and on the 5th anniversary of its historic decision to expand Wi-Fi into 6 GHz for increased capacity to support the growth of wireless devices and new innovative use cases. As a key advocate of the 6 GHz band, we’re seeing many customers take advantage of these capabilities in their products using our Wi-Fi chips with lower latency and better co-existence with other wireless technologies. As devices become more intelligent and the need for real-time device communication increases, Infineon will continue to work closely with Wi-Fi Alliance, regulatory bodies and partners to ensure our customers have solutions that meet their growing needs across automotive, industrial, enterprise and consumer IoT applications.” –Sivaram Trikutam, SVP of Wireless Connectivity,
Infineon Technologies
"I can't believe it's been 5 years since the joint Intel-Broadcom
demo
at the FCC offices in Washington D.C., where we were the first to demonstrate the benefits of 6 GHz Wi-Fi. I remember Chairman Pai sharing our view that 6 GHz is a vital resource, enabling unparalleled Wi-Fi performance and multi-gigabit speeds throughout the home due to clean spectrum and up to 320 MHz channels. I am excited to say that 5 years later, we are seeing 6 GHz adoption exceeding expectations through broad industry collaboration supported by Wi-Fi Alliance certification." – Eric A. McLaughlin, VP, Client Computing Group, GM, Connectivity Solutions Group,
Intel Corporation
"The FCC's historic 6 GHz decision has driven innovation and product investments, significantly improving connectivity for consumers across the U.S. On the 5th anniversary of this decision, MaxLinear congratulates the FCC and the industry on these advancements. Shortly after the decision, MaxLinear launched its first Wi-Fi 6E product, laying the foundation for our next-generation, industry-leading tri-band single-chip, which includes Wi-Fi 7 baseband and radio processing for all three bands. The high level of integration in MaxLinear's Wi-Fi 7 single-chip lowers costs for consumers while fully unlocking the potential of the 6 GHz band by improving throughput and reducing latency. These tremendous advancements in Wi-Fi were made possible by the FCC's decision. MaxLinear remains committed to driving innovation and delivering exceptional experiences for customers and service providers.” – Puneet Sethi, Vice President of
MaxLinear’s
Network Infrastructure and Carrier Business.
“Five years ago, the FCC's historic decision to open the 6 GHz spectrum to Wi-Fi marked a transformative milestone in wireless connectivity. Qualcomm Technologies is proud to have been part of a group of industry visionaries who played a pivotal role in driving this change. As we celebrate this anniversary, we reflect on the profound impact this decision has had in unlocking Wi-Fi's full potential with Wi-Fi 6E, Wi-Fi 7 and beyond, enabling unprecedented connectivity and performance for consumers, businesses, and industries. We look forward to continuing our journey of innovation, ensuring Wi-Fi remains a cornerstone of global connectivity.” – Rahul Patel, Group General Manager, Connectivity, Broadband & Networking (CBN),
Qualcomm Technologies, Inc.
“Securing 6 GHz spectrum for the Wi-Fi market not only anchored massive improvements in throughput and latency for consumers/users but also catapulted the technology advancement in semiconductor process, design, and packaging. This additional spectrum supports the continued Wi-Fi standard evolution and ability to accelerate use-case applications fueled by edge compute and AI advancements. These advancements are not just about higher speeds; they are about creating smarter, more responsive environments that can support the growing diversity and density of today's digital landscape.  As we celebrate this milestone anniversary, we recognize the profound impact these technologies have had on our ability to connect, communicate and innovate. The future of wireless is here and brighter than ever." – Tony Testa, General Manager, Connectivity Components Business Unit,
Qorvo, Inc.
“The action from the FCC was a game-changer, ushering in a new era of enterprise connectivity by paving the way for Wi-Fi 7, which delivers unprecedented levels of speed, reliability, and ultra-low latency for the modern digital enterprise. At RUCKUS Networks, CommScope, we recognized early on that the 6 GHz band would become the backbone of next-gen enterprise wireless. Since that historic 2020 ruling, we’ve been proud to introduce the most complete line of AI-Driven indoor and outdoor Wi-Fi 7 solutions capitalizing on the value of 6 GHz. Opening the band opened up a world of new possibilities and we’re excited to be a part of the revolution.” – Mittal Parekh, Senior Director, Products,
RUCKUS Networks,
CommScope
“The introduction of 6 GHz Wi-Fi five years ago paved the way for Skyworks to continue advancing our mission of connecting everyone and everything, all the time. As the market continues to evolve and new bandwidth-heavy applications are introduced, we’re proud to be driving and shaping the future for global Wi-Fi adoption through our participation in the Wi-Fi Alliance.” – Chung Liang Lee, director of product marketing for broad markets at
Skyworks
“The FCC’s landmark decision to open the 6 GHz band five years ago transformed the Wi-Fi landscape, unlocking unprecedented capacity and paving the way for Wi-Fi 6E and now Wi-Fi 7. title: Unlocking the power of collaboration: Interoperability Event highlights from Tokyo
content:
Earlier this year, Wi-Fi Alliance® hosted its 2025 Asia Member Meeting in Tokyo, Japan, bringing together industry leaders and innovators to discuss the latest advancements in Wi-Fi®. A standout session from the event was the panel on
Interoperability Events
— critical gatherings where Wi-Fi Alliance members test the functionality and compatibility of their Wi-Fi products in real-world scenarios. These events are more than just technical exercises; they are a cornerstone of the collaboration that drives the Wi-Fi ecosystem forward.
In this blog, we have distilled the panel’s rich discussion, offering a glimpse into how Interoperability Events take shape, their impact on the industry, and what is on the horizon for 2025.
How Interoperability Events come to life
The panel kicked off with Peng Yan, Wireless Technologist at Wi-Fi Alliance and primary point of contact for Interoperability Events, walking through the anatomy of an Interoperability Event. These events come in two formats: member-driven and staff-driven.
Member-driven events:
An example of these would be Interoperability Events focused on Wi-Fi HaLow™ and Wi-Fi Location™. Here, members take the lead, organizing the testing themselves while staff provide logistical support — venues, network cables, and whatever else is needed to make it happen.
Staff-driven events:
These start with a clear objective, often sparked by member feedback. For instance, when operators flagged roaming as a persistent pain point, Wi-Fi Alliance responded with a series of dedicated roaming events. Similarly, Internet of Things (IoT) devices that run on batteries require low-power functionality, prompting an event for testing interoperability with different power saving modes. This event helped Wi-Fi Alliance improve its Power Saving Features certification.
Staff identify the event’s theme, utilize testing labs like RDL in Santa Clara or collaborate with Authorized Test Labs (ATLs) worldwide, and brainstorm test scenarios with members. From there, it is all about logistics — simulating environments (such as office or home setups) and running pre-event calls with vendors to align on test scenarios. During the event week, participants execute tests, collect data, and share feedback to refine future events.
The numbers tell the story
Since September 2023, Wi-Fi Alliance has hosted Interoperability Events with more than 100 member companies participating, testing more than 450 end-product devices (not just reference designs). Gaurav Jain, VP of Technology at Wi-Fi Alliance, highlighted a key goal: doubling participation to amplify the industry-wide benefits.
“Interoperability is not just about technology — it is about collaboration,” Gaurav noted, echoing a recurring theme. These events bring together a diverse set of stakeholders — including device manufacturers, OS vendors, enterprise solution providers, and operators — to evaluate products and device implementations in deployment-relevant environments. They provide a collaborative platform to uncover compatibility issues, bridge gaps across the ecosystem, and ensure that Wi-Fi continues to deliver on its promise of seamless, reliable connectivity.
Real-world impact: Voices from the panel
The panelists shared how these events have shaped their work:
Mark Hamilton, Networking Standards Director, RUCKUS Networks:
“We passed all the tests quite easily, but not to the level of performance that we expected or wanted, and we used the Interoperability Events to solve that problem and take the next step beyond what the test cases require.” Mark emphasized the importance of working through MLO operations and behavior during the Wi-Fi 7 events, going further than what is possible during plugfests.
David Halasz, VP of Standards, Morse Micro:
Reflecting on a recent Wi-Fi HaLow event, David emphasized that even though they had to scale back activities to focus on certification testing due to spectrum constraints, “the important thing was that we were in China, and it was definitely the Interoperability Event that gave us an opportunity to perform outreach.”
Dorothy Stanley, HPE Fellow, Aruba:
“Without the Interoperability Event, we would not have had client vendors in one place to test efficiently, find the errors, and then go back and incorporate that into our implementation.” Dorothy also traced the evolution of Wi-Fi Location testing, noting how Interoperability Events have driven sub-meter accuracy and improved vendor implementations since 2018.
Guoqi Cui, Senior Test Engineer, Google:
Guoqi shared a specific Wi-Fi 7 debugging win, where an event revealed a fast-roaming conflict affecting MLO with enterprise access points. “What we found is that for an enterprise system, normally people enable fast roaming, so we discovered that the issue is really caused by that flag.”
To add to the experiences of the rest of the panel, Peng recounted how testing at a WPA3™ event shaped the compatibility mode solution, now an important part of the WPA3 program: “We had transition mode issues with many devices, so at the WPA3 event, we tested two solutions — compatibility mode (RSN Override) and multiple BSSIDs under one SSID — across over 100 devices. The goal was to ensure legacy devices could connect while newer ones used WPA3. Results led to the adoption of RSN Override, with compatibility mode launching last year to fix transition mode problems.”
Looking ahead: The Interoperability Lab and 2025 plans
Exciting developments are on the horizon. Wi-Fi Alliance is building an Interoperability Lab at RDL in Santa Clara, set to open to members in 2025. With 15+ Wi-Fi 6/Wi-Fi 7 routers, 130+ client devices (laptops, smartphones, smart home, etc.), and multiple ISP backhauls, it is designed for stringent testing of real-world scenarios.
For 2025, confirmed events include:
Wi-Fi Location
: April 28 – May 2 ∙ Santa Clara
Security
: May 5 – May 9 ∙ Santa Clara & Taipei; May 12 – May 16 ∙ Beijing
Wi-Fi 6 and Wi-Fi 7
: September 8 – September 12 ∙ Santa Clara, Taipei, and Beijing
Why Interoperability Events matter
The panel underscored that interoperability testing is not just about passing a checklist — it is about ensuring Wi-Fi works for everyone, everywhere. It also highlighted that there is no one-solution-fits-all approach to interoperability; effective testing must account for diverse needs of devices, networks, and real-world deployment scenarios. From fixing roaming issues to boosting Wi-Fi 7 performance, these events shape standards, inform certifications, and strengthen the foundation of an ever-evolving Wi-Fi ecosystem.
Interoperability Insights
, a new Wi-Fi Alliance publication for members, details actionable insights from Interoperability Events, offering significant value to members and the broader industry, even for those who did not participate in an event. With the new lab and multiple events scheduled for 2025, there has never been a better time to get involved.
If you are a Wi-Fi Alliance member eager to join an Interoperability Event, head over to our
Interoperability Events page
to register. If you would like more information on joining Wi-Fi Alliance so you can participate,
send us a message
.

title: Episode 79: 5 years of 6 GHz: celebrating a Wi-Fi® milestone with Alex Roytblat of Wi-Fi Alliance®
content:
In this episode, we welcome Alex Roytblat, Vice President, Worldwide Regulatory Affairs at Wi-Fi Alliance, to The Signal to commemorate the fifth anniversary of the FCC's landmark decision to open the 6 GHz band to Wi-Fi. Alex explains that this was the most significant expansion of spectrum for Wi-Fi in decades, which effectively doubled the spectrum for Wi-Fi in U.S., and ushered in the development of a world of new technology, including Wi-Fi 6E and Wi-Fi 7. We talk about how 6 GHz has opened the doors to innovation, including telemedicine, extended reality, and industrial manufacturing, and we learn how spectrum policy will evolve to support future Wi-Fi generations. Tune in to learn more as we celebrate the historic decision that brought Wi-Fi into a new era.

title: Wi-Fi Alliance Messaging Collective Highlights
content:
Wi-Fi Alliance®  
Messaging Collective 
 
Introducing the Messaging Collective 
Wi-Fi Alliance® is introducing the Messaging Collective to coordinate marketing, communications, public relations, product 
marketing, and company leaders to develop, align, and refine messaging on topics shaping our industry. The goal of the 
Messaging Collective is to ensure that the Wi-Fi® industry has a unified voice — supported by real-world examples from 
our 900+ member companies — that resonates with target audiences. As a contributor to this group, you will help 
influence the direction of Wi-Fi topics worldwide and position your company at the forefront of emerging technologies. 
Why join? 
This initiative is an opportunity for your company to: 
• Lead the industry: Collaborate within Wi-Fi Alliance to craft powerful, unified messaging that reflects industry 
priorities and supports narratives that resonate with target audiences and key stakeholders 
• Define Wi-Fi’s role: Help define Wi-Fi’s role in emerging technologies and markets such as artificial intelligence 
(AI), 6G convergence, cybersecurity, quantum computing, and more  
• Gain company visibility: Showcase your company’s activities in these areas through co-marketing and thought 
leadership 
• Publish important resources: Work with Wi-Fi Alliance and vendor partners to publish important materials related 
to the topics defined in the Messaging Collective to gain broader global awareness 
Key program elements 
1. Centralized collaboration: A space for members to contribute ideas, use cases, case studies, and insights, and 
refine industry positioning 
2. Shared resources: Access to messaging frameworks and talking points 
3. Industry voice alignment: Ensures that the industry speaks with one voice when it matters 
4. Strategic guidance: Helps create narratives that resonate with target audiences 
5. Marketing outputs: Facilitates group discussion about materials (e.g., papers, case studies, one-pagers) needed 
to influence different audiences, regions, or platforms 
6. Publishing house: Opportunities to engage preferred vendors to publish and promote identified materials 
Get involved now

title: Episode 77: Wi-Fi 7 unlocks speed and sustainability with Quentin Lebeau of SoftAtHome
content:
In this episode, we welcome Quentin Lebeau, Product Marketing Manager at SoftAtHome, to discuss their recent Wi-Fi 7 gateway launch with Swisscom. Quentin delves into the rising consumer demand for cutting-edge technology, making Wi-Fi 7's key capabilities of higher speeds, lower latency, and increased reliability even more appealing to consumers. Quentin explains that Wi-Fi 7 also enables the use of embedded AI, allowing gateways to optimize bandwidth allocation, which is vital to delivering a higher quality of service for consumers. But innovation isn't just about performance - Quentin shares that more consumers are also interested in sustainability efforts, and we learn that the new gateway's subscriber-enabled low power mode reduces power consumption up to 98%. Tune in to learn more, including Quentin's insight on the value of consistent user experiences for service providers.

Technical Note: Achieving secure network connectivity for all devices  v1.0 
 
© 2025 Wi-Fi Alliance. All Rights Reserved.  
Used with the permission of Wi-Fi Alliance under the terms as stated in this document. 
Page 2 of 6 
1 Introduction 
This document provides guidelines and recommendations for achieving secure network connectivity for all devices. Each 
device can use the most secure configuration of the robust security network (RSN) that it and the network can support, 
while allowing devices with other capabilities to also connect using other security configurations that they support. This 
allows devices with different security capabilities of different generations (e.g., Wi-Fi 4, Wi‑Fi 5, Wi‑Fi 6, & Wi‑Fi 7) to 
connect seamlessly to the same network. This document provides descriptions of the interoperability issues found with 
WPA3™ and some recommended mitigations based on the WPA3 specification [1]. 
2 Problem 
One of the main strengths of Wi-Fi technology is the ability to support network connectivity for devices with different 
capabilities and generations (e.g., Wi-Fi 4, Wi‑Fi 5, Wi‑Fi 6, & Wi‑Fi 7). The robust security network (RSN) defined in IEEE 
Std 802.11 [2] provides a flexible framework to allow these different devices to connect securely. With the roll-out of 
WPA3 and the growth of Wi-Fi devices in home, public, and enterprise devices, a number of interoperability issues have 
been discovered.  
With the successful adoption of WPA2-Personal (single PSK AKM and either one or two pairwise cipher suites 
TKIP/CCMP as an RSN configuration on an AP), some implementations exhibit connectivity issues when the RSN 
configuration advertised by an AP does not exactly match the WPA2-Personal configuration. 
The following issues are some of the problems that have been identified for STAs: 
• WPA2 STA not supporting more than one AKM advertised by an AP – Some implementations will only 
attempt to associate if there is a single AKM advertised by an AP.  
• STA not supporting more than two AKMs advertised by an AP – Some implementations will not connect if 
more than two AKMs are advertised by an AP.  
• STA not supporting more than one cipher suite advertised by an AP – Some implementations will not 
connect if two or more unicast cipher suites are advertised by an AP. 
• STA copying fields from AP’s RSNE – Some implementations copy the fields advertised by an AP in its RSN 
rather than selecting field values for an RSNE based on the configured network profile. This can result in a STA 
negotiating capabilities that it does not support. 
• STA not supporting RSNXE in EAPOL-Key msg 3/4 – An AP needs to include the RSNXE (if supported) in 
EAPOL-Key message 3. Some implementations cannot process the message when the RSNXE is included. This 
results in a connection failure. 
• STA SNonce updates with EAPOL-Key retransmissions – Some implementations update the SNonce for each 
EAPOL-Key message 2 transmission rather than for each instance of the 4-way handshake. This can result in a 
connection failure. 
The following issue has been identified for APs: 
• AP not supporting RSNXE in EAPOL-Key msg 2/4 – A STA needs to include the RSNXE (if supported) in 
EAPOL-Key message 2. Some implementations cannot process the message when the RSNXE is included. This 
results in a connection failure. 
The following issue has been identified for both APs and STAs: 
• Mismatch in PTK derivation due to incorrect capability negotiation – The PTK derivation has been modified 
based on capabilities negotiated using fields in the RSNE and RSNXE.  
The following issue is due to constraints in the protocol: 
• MFPR=1 advertised by an AP – A STA that does not support Protected Management Frames (PMF) cannot 
interpret MFPR=1 and cannot determine that it will not be able to connect to an AP that advertises MFPR=1. If 
there are a mixture of APs in a home environment that set MFPR=1, the STA will not be able to connect to those 
APs. 
 
Technical Note: Achieving secure network connectivity for all devices  v1.0 
 
© 2025 Wi-Fi Alliance. All Rights Reserved.  
Used with the permission of Wi-Fi Alliance under the terms as stated in this document. 
Page 3 of 6 
3 Recommended mitigations 
Continued interoperability between STAs and APs involves creating a robust implementation of RSN. This is particularly 
important as RSN features are extended to support newer security capabilities and features such as those defined in 
WPA3 and new security requirements defined in Wi-Fi 7. While interoperability testing is essential, it is also important to 
ensure that an RSN implementation is robust for a product being developed.  
A STA is provisioned with a network profile that contains, at a minimum, an SSID and credential. When an AP advertises 
multiple AKMs, cipher suites, and other RSN capabilities, the STA needs identify RSN parameters that match the AP 
security configuration in order to connect. RSN parameters include: 
• one AKM suite 
• one pairwise cipher suite 
• one group data cipher suite 
• negotiate PMF (true/false)  
• one group management cipher suite, when PMF is negotiated 
• use SAE hash-to-element (SAE H2E) (true/false), when an SAE AKM is negotiated 
• other security parameters in the RSNE and RSNXE capabilities 
APs can advertise multiple AKMs and multiple cipher suites depending on the security requirements for the Wi-Fi network 
and allow devices with different security capabilities (e.g., WPA2 and WPA3) to connect to the same network. A STA that 
selects the network advertised by an AP needs to select a single RSN policy that matches the AP based on its 
capabilities. 
As new protocol elements are advertised by APs and included in the 4-way handshake, the STA or AP implementations 
need to ignore AKMs, cipher suites, capabilities, and elements they do not support in order to successfully connect. 
The following requirements must be satisfied to ensure RSN interoperability and security based on [1] and [2] (note that in 
the requirements below, the acronyms are defined in [1]): 
• A STA or AP MUST NOT transmit RSNE/RSNOE/RSNO2E payloads that do not meet the format required by the 
WPA3 specification [1] and the 802.11 standard [2] 
▪ A STA or AP MUST set the Version field to 01 00 
▪ A STA or AP MUST NOT generate a 1-octet Version field 
▪ A STA or AP MUST NOT generate 1-octet Pairwise Cipher Suite/AKM Suite/PMKID Count fields, where 
present 
▪ A STA or AP MUST NOT include fewer (or more) items in the Pairwise Cipher Suite/AKM Suite/PMKID List 
field, where present, than specified in the corresponding Count field, where present 
▪ A STA or AP MUST NOT generate a 1-octet RSN Capabilities field, where present 
▪ A STA MUST NOT copy the RSN Capabilities field received from the AP, where present. The STA MUST 
specify its own RSN capabilities, where present 
▪ A STA or AP MUST generate little-endian Version, Pairwise Cipher Suite/AKM Suite/PMKID Count and RSN 
Capabilities fields, where present 
▪ A STA MUST NOT include more than one pairwise cipher suite selector or AKM suite selector (i.e., if the 
Pairwise Cipher / AKM Suite Count field is present it MUST be set to 01 00) 
▪ An AP MUST NOT set the Pairwise Cipher / AKM Suite Count field, where present, to 00 00 
▪ An AP MUST NOT include any PMKIDs (if the PMKID Count field is present it MUST be set to 00 00) in 
Beacon and Probe Response frames  
▪ Note: A STA or AP might be more tolerant of malformed elements on receive. But on transmit, the STA or AP 
MUST strictly conform to the WPA3 specification [1] and the 802.11 standard [2] 
• A STA or AP MUST NOT transmit RSNXE/RSNXOE payloads that do not meet the format required by the WPA3 
specification [1] and the 802.11 standard [2] 
▪ A STA MUST NOT copy the RSNXE/RSNXOE received from the AP. The STA MUST specify its own 
capabilities, where present 
• A STA or AP that parses received RSNE or (RSN overriding only) RSNOE/RSNO2E payloads that meet the 
format required by the WPA3 specification [1] and the 802.11 standard [2] MUST do so correctly 
▪ A STA MUST accept any number of AKM suite selectors (NOT just 1 or 2) 
Technical Note: Achieving secure network connectivity for all devices  v1.0 
 
© 2025 Wi-Fi Alliance. All Rights Reserved.  
Used with the permission of Wi-Fi Alliance under the terms as stated in this document. 
Page 4 of 6 
▪ A STA MUST identify and select its preferred AKM irrespective of its position in the list (NOT just if it is the 
first or last one) 
▪ A STA MUST ignore all AKM suite selectors that it does not recognize (i.e., MUST NOT refuse/ignore an 
RSNE/RSNOE/RSNO2E just because it signals an AKM that it does not recognize, among others that it does 
recognize) 
▪ A STA MUST accept any number of pairwise cipher suite selectors (NOT just 1 or 2) 
▪ A STA MUST identify and select its preferred cipher irrespective of its position in the list (NOT just if it is the 
first or last one) 
▪ A STA MUST ignore all pairwise cipher suite selectors that it does not recognize (i.e., MUST NOT 
refuse/ignore an RSNE/RSNOE/RSNO2E just because it signals a pairwise cipher that it does not recognize, 
among others that it does recognize) 
▪ A STA or AP MUST ignore all RSN Capabilities field bits that it does not recognize (i.e., MUST NOT 
refuse/ignore an RSNE/RSNOE/RSNO2E just because it signals capabilities that it does not recognize) 
▪ An AP MUST accept any number of PMKIDs (NOT just 0 or 1) 
▪ An AP MUST ignore all PMKIDs that it does not recognize (i.e., MUST NOT refuse/ignore an RSNE just 
because it signals a PMKID that it does not recognize or signals no PMKID that it does recognize), except (a) 
if the STA used Open System authentication and then indicated an SAE AKM in the RSNE in the 
(Re)Association Request frame (i.e., SAE PMKSA caching), in which case the AP MUST reject the 
(re)association with STATUS_INVALID_PMKID if it doesn't recognize any of the PMKIDs as corresponding to 
a PMKSA with the same SAE AKM, and except (b) for FILS (which is an optional capability of Wi‑Fi Optimized 
Connectivity [4]) (see the 802.11 standard [2] for details). 
▪ A STA or AP MUST ignore all fields it does not recognize or use (e.g., a non-PMF STA MUST ignore the 
Group Management Cipher Suite field where present) 
▪ A STA or AP MUST accept defaults for missing fields, per the 802.11 standard [2] 
▪ Note: In general, MFPC=1 will be signaled so the only field that will typically be missing is the Group 
Management Cipher Suite field (because the default is used). However, in the most extreme case the RSNE 
for an Enterprise connection using 802.1X with SHA-1 with CCMP-128 and without PMF might include only 
the Version field 
• A STA or AP that parses received RSNXE or (RSN overriding only) RSNXOE payloads that meet the format 
required by the WPA3 specification [1] and the 802.11 standard [2] MUST do so correctly 
▪ A STA or AP MUST accept any Field length field value (0 to 15, i.e., 1 to 16 octets in the Extended RSN 
Capabilities field) (NOT just 0 or 1); an AP MUST NOT refuse/ignore an RSNXE just because it has more 
octets than the AP advertised in its RSNXE/RSNXOE 
▪ A STA or AP MUST accept any octets after the Extended RSN Capabilities field (i.e., the Length field in the 
RSNXE/RSNXOE might be 255) (i.e., MUST NOT refuse/ignore an RSNXE/RSNXOE just because it has 
extra octets) 
▪ A STA or AP MUST ignore all bits that it does not recognize (i.e., MUST NOT refuse/ignore an 
RSNXE/RSNXOE just because it signals capabilities that it does not recognize) 
• A STA or AP MUST guard against downgrade (and other) attacks as required by the WPA3 specification [1] and 
the 802.11 standard [2] 
▪ A STA or AP MUST check the MICs in (or, when using an AEAD cipher, decryption status for) messages 2, 3 
and 4 of the 4-way handshake (4WH) and MUST ignore the message on failure 
▪ A STA or AP MUST check the MICs in (or, when using an AEAD cipher, decryption status for) messages 1 
and 2 of the group key handshake (GKH) and MUST ignore the message on failure 
▪ An AP MUST check that an RSNE is present in both the (Re)Association Request frame and message 2 of 
the 4WH, and is identical. If an RSNE is present in one but not the other, or is not identical, the AP MUST 
abort the 4WH 
▪ An AP MUST check that an RSNXE is either not present in the (Re)Association Request frame nor message 
2 of the 4WH, or that it is present in both and identical. If an RSNXE is present in one but not the other, or is 
not identical, the AP MUST abort the 4WH 
▪ A STA MUST check that an RSNE is present in both the Beacon / Probe Response frames and message 3 of 
the 4WH, and identical (for each link, for an MLO (re)association). If an RSNE is present in one but not the 
other, or is not identical, the STA MUST abort the 4WH 
▪ A STA MUST check that an RSNXE is either not present in either the Beacon / Probe Response frames nor 
message 3 of the 4WH, or that it is present in both and identical (for each link, for an MLO (re)association). If 
an RSNXE is present in one but not the other, or is not identical, the STA MUST abort the 4WH 
Technical Note: Achieving secure network connectivity for all devices  v1.0 
 
© 2025 Wi-Fi Alliance. All Rights Reserved.  
Used with the permission of Wi-Fi Alliance under the terms as stated in this document. 
Page 5 of 6 
▪ A STA using RSN parameters selected from an RSNOE, RSNO2E or RSNXOE (i.e., using RSN overriding) 
MUST include an RSN Selection element in the (Re)Association Request frame and an RSN Selection 
element and an SNonce cookie in message 2 of the 4WH 
▪ A STA using RSN overriding MUST check that the RSNE and (where present) RSNOE, RSNO2E, RSNXE 
and RSNXOE in message 3 of the 4WH are identical with those received in the Beacon and Probe Response 
frames (for each link, for an MLO (re)association). If the RSNE/RSNOE/RSNO2E/RSNXE/RSNXOE are 
present in one but not the other, or is not identical (for each link, for an MLO (re)association), the STA MUST 
abort the 4WH 
▪ An AP advertising an RSNOE or RSNO2E (i.e., using RSN overriding) MUST check that an RSN Selection 
element is either not present in the (Re)Association Request frame nor message 2 of the 4WH, or that it is 
present in both and identical. If the RSN Selection element is present in one but not the other, or is not 
identical, the AP MUST abort the 4WH 
▪ Note: If the RSN Selection element is present in neither, the STA is not using RSN overriding 
▪ An AP using RSN overriding MUST use the RSN Selection element, where present, to identify which of the 
RSNE, RSNOE, and RSNO2E  the STA is using for the (re)association 
▪ An AP (MLD) using RSN overriding and MLO MUST include the same RSNO2E in Beacon and Probe 
Response frames on all operating channels of its affiliated APs 
▪ If an AP (MLD) using RSN overriding and MLO transmits an RSNXOE, it MUST include the same RSNXOE in 
Beacon and Probe Response frames on all operating channels of its affiliated APs. Otherwise, if the AP 
(MLD) transmits an RSNXE, the AP MUST include the same RSNXE in all Beacon and Probe Response 
frames on all operating channels of its affiliated APs 
▪ Note: An AP (MLD) using RSN overriding might transmit no RSNXOEs and no RSNXEs 
▪ A STA using RSN overriding MUST use only one of the RSNE/RSNOE/RSNO2E (i.e., MUST NOT use some 
fields from one of these elements and some other fields from another of these elements) 
▪ A STA using RSN overriding and MLO MUST use the RSNO2E where present; it MUST NOT use the 
RSNOE or RSNE, where present, for an MLO (re)association when an RSNO2E is advertised by an AP 
▪ A STA using RSN overriding MUST use the RSNXOE where present; it MUST NOT use the RSNXE, where 
present, for a (re)association when an RSNXOE is advertised by an AP 
▪ A STA using RSN overriding MUST NOT include an RSNOE/RSNO2E/RSNXOE in the (Re)Association 
Request frame or in message 2 of the 4WH 
▪ An AP using RSN overriding MUST NOT include an RSNOE/RSNO2E/RSNXOE in the (Re)Association 
Response frame, except for the Reassociation Response frame sent under Fast Transition (FT) (note not 
Association Response frame), where an AP using RSN overriding MUST include all the 
RSNOEs/RSNO2Es/RSNXOEs that it advertised in the Beacon and Probe Response frames 
▪ Note: An AP advertises the same RSNXE in the (Re)Association Response frame as in the Beacon and 
Probe Response frames, where present, even if the STA indicated (using the RSN Selection element) that it 
is using the RSNXOE from the Beacon and Probe Response frames, where present. An AP generally does 
not include the RSNE in the (Re)Association Response frame; for exceptions (including FT [2], Opportunistic 
Wireless Encryption (OWE) [2] [5] and FILS [2] [4])  
• Other requirements 
▪ A STA or AP MUST accept KDEs and elements it recognizes in any position in the Key Data field of all 
messages of the 4WH and of the GKH (NOT just in a fixed order) 
▪ A STA or AP MUST ignore all KDEs and elements it does not recognize in any position in the Key Data field 
in all messages of the 4WH and of the GKH (i.e., MUST NOT refuse/ignore a message just because it 
contains a KDE or element it does not recognize or because the KDEs and elements it recognizes have a 
KDE or element it does not recognize between them) 
▪ Note: An AP might omit certain KDEs and elements (including RSNOE/RSNO2E/RSNXOE) from message 3 
of the 4WH if message 2 did not contain an SNonce cookie 
▪ A STA or AP MUST set the Reserved field to all-zeros in all messages of the 4WH and of the GKH it 
transmits and MUST ignore the Reserved field in all messages of the 4WH and of the GKH it receives (i.e., 
MUST NOT refuse/ignore a message just because the Reserved field is non-zero) 
▪ A STA or AP MUST NOT have limits on the field sizes it is able to process, except absolute limits implied by 
the size of length fields (e.g., a STA or AP MUST accept an RSNE/RSNOE/RSNO2E with 255 octets in the 
Information field) 
▪ A STA MUST NOT change the SNonce field when retransmitting message 2 of the 4WH, for a given 4WH 
▪ An AP MUST NOT advertise AKM suite selectors (6 GHz only) in the 6 GHz band that are forbidden in the 6 
GHz band or (RSN overriding only) in an RSNOE/RSNO2E that are forbidden in an RSNOE/RSNO2E

▪ Note (MLO only): An AP might advertise AKM suite selectors that are forbidden for MLO, but the forbidden 
AKM suite selectors MUST NOT be accepted as part of MLO (re)associations 
▪ A STA MUST NOT select an AKM suite selector that is forbidden (6 GHz only) in the 6 GHz band  
▪ An AP MUST NOT include an RSNXOE if it advertises neither an RSNOE nor an RSNO2E (RSN overriding 
only) 
▪ An AP MUST advertise the same RSNE/RSNOE/RSNO2E/RSNXE/RSNXOE (where present) in Beacon and 
Probe Response frames, on a given channel 
▪ An AP MUST NOT advertise cipher suites that are forbidden in the WPA3 specification [1] and the 802.11 
standard [2] 
▪ For SAE authentication, hash-to-element (H2E) MUST be used if both STA and AP support the capability as 
advertised through the RSNXE or (RSN overriding only) RSNXOE 
▪ An AP that advertises, or a STA that selects, SAE with MLO or in the 6 GHz band MUST support and 
advertise H2E 
▪ An AP that does not advertise MFPR = 1 MUST NOT reject a STA just because it did not signal MFPC = 1, 
unless the AP’s policy, the WPA3 specification [1] or the 802.11 standard [2] requires PMF, or the STA 
selected an SAE AKM  
▪ Note: Certain features might require PMF (e.g., Wi-Fi 7, Wi‑Fi Agile Multiband [3]) and might not be available 
to a STA if PMF was not negotiated 
▪ A STA that does not signal MFPR = 1 MUST NOT reject an AP just because it does not advertise MFPC = 1, 
unless the STA’s policy, the WPA3 specification [1] or the 802.11 standard [2] requires PMF, or the STA 
selects an SAE AKM 
▪ Note: Certain features might require PMF (e.g., Wi-Fi 7, Wi‑Fi Agile Multiband [3]) and might not be available 
to a STA if PMF was not negotiated 
▪ An AP that advertises MFPR = 1 MUST advertise MFPC = 1 and MUST reject a STA that did not signal 
MFPC = 1, but MUST NOT reject a STA just because it did not signal MFPR = 1 
▪ A STA that requires PMF MUST signal MFPC = 1 and MUST NOT attempt to connect to an AP that does not 
advertise MFPC = 1 but MUST NOT reject an AP just because it does not advertise MFPR = 1 
▪ An AP or STA using RSN overriding with FT has additional requirements; see the WPA3 specification [1]

title: WPA3™ Deployment Options Highlights
content:
Driving widespread adoption of WPA3 
Wi-Fi Alliance® is committed to ensuring the long-term migration and broadest possible use of WPA3™ across all  
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED® devices. WPA3 support has been required in all new Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices since 2020 and its use 
is mandatory in the 6 GHz band. Wi-Fi Alliance strongly recommends that deployers and users configure Wi-Fi 
networks for WPA3 whenever possible.   
WPA3 transition mode allows connection to either WPA3 or WPA2™ 
Many older devices that do not support WPA3 still exist in large and small networks around the world. In order to 
support both WPA3 and WPA2™ devices in the same network, WPA3 includes a built-in transition mode. This 
transition mode allows client devices that support 
WPA3 to connect with WPA3 while older devices 
connect with WPA2 (see Figure 1). Unfortunately, 
Wi-Fi Alliance is aware of some deployment 
environments where legacy or uncertified devices 
experience interoperability issues with a network 
configured for WPA3 transition mode. 
 
Alternatives to WPA3 transition mode 
One alternative is to configure two SSIDs (two 
networks) on the access point (AP), one with WPA3 
and the other with WPA2. Such a network should be 
configured with different passwords on each SSID 
(see Figure 2).  
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
 
             Figure 1: WPA3-Personal transition mode 
WPA3™ deployment options 
WPA3-Personal offers numerous benefits 
WPA3-Personal brings better protections to individual 
users by providing more robust password-based 
authentication, even when users choose passwords that 
fall short of typical complexity recommendations. This 
capability is enabled through Simultaneous 
Authentication of Equals (SAE). The technology is 
resistant to offline dictionary attacks where an adversary 
attempts to determine a network password by trying 
possible passwords without further network interaction. 
• Natural password selection: Allows users to 
choose passwords that are easier to remember 
• Ease of use: Delivers enhanced protections with 
no change to the way users connect to a network 
• Forward secrecy: Protects data traffic even if a 
password is compromised after the data was 
transmitted 
Figure 2: Network with two SSIDs 
 
© 2024 Wi-Fi Alliance. All rights reserved. Wi-Fi, the Wi-Fi logo, the Wi-Fi CERTIFIED logo, and other marks are trademarks of Wi-Fi Alliance.  
If that solution does not work for your deployment, Wi-Fi Alliance has released a new compatibility mode for 
environments that must support problematic older devices but where proven alternatives to WPA3 transition mode 
such as multiple SSIDs are not appropriate. 
 
The new WPA3-Personal compatibility mode hides WPA3 from older devices, allowing all client devices to connect. 
Only those devices that support the new capability (RSN overriding or RSNO) will be exposed to the WPA3 security 
protocol, mitigating the network connection issues encountered by older, uncertified client devices in the presence 
of a network configured for WPA3-Personal transition mode and ensuring that all clients can connect to the 
network. Older devices will connect with WPA2, while updated 
devices will see and connect with WPA3 (see Figure 3). 
 
This new compatibility mode will require updates to existing    
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED APs. In order to use this mode, configure the 
network’s AP for WPA3-Personal compatibility mode. The 
network may appear as a WPA2-Personal network, depending on 
the capabilities of each client device. Client devices that support 
the new capability will connect with the benefits of WPA3-Personal, 
while older client devices will connect with WPA2-Personal.  
  
 
 
 
 
 
 
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED: Technology to trust 
Since 2000, Wi-Fi Alliance has been driving the adoption and evolution of Wi-Fi through the Wi-Fi CERTIFIED 
program. The Wi-Fi CERTIFIED logo designates products with proven interoperability, backward compatibility, and 
the highest industry-standard security protections in place. Wi-Fi CERTIFIED devices can communicate with previous 
and future generations of Wi-Fi technologies, enabling a seamless, interoperable experience with a multitude of 
other Wi-Fi devices for years to come. 
 
 
 
 
Learn more: www.wi-fi.org/discover-wi-fi/security 
Device implementation considerations for WPA3-Personal compatibility mode 
APs: Wi-Fi Alliance recommends that device vendors use the term “WPA3-Personal compatibility” or “WPA3 
compatibility” in the user configuration interface 
Client devices: Wi-Fi Alliance recommends that, if implemented, support for the new capability should be 
invisible to the user and enabled without a user configuration option to disable 
Figure 2: WPA3-Personal compatibility mode

title: Wi-Fi CERTIFIED Wi-Fi Direct® Highlights
content:
Wi-Fi CERTIFIED Wi-Fi Direct® 
Highlights 
Connecting devices nearby 
Driven by the desire of users to easily connect their devices, Wi-Fi Direct® provides peer-to-
peer (P2P) technologies that allow devices to connect to each other using their Wi-Fi® 
interfaces without the need of an access point (AP) or Wi-Fi hotspot. This means users on 
the go can wirelessly print documents, share screens, share data, sync files, and display 
information from devices like notebooks, smartphones, and tablets.    
Wi-Fi Direct offers tremendous value to users, not just by providing extended range, high 
throughput, and robust security, but also by increasing user mobility, productivity, and ease-
of-use.   
Wi-Fi Direct® features and advances 
Wi-Fi Direct uses the existing IEEE 802.11 standard and AP/client device topology to set up a P2P group or a P2P 
connection. One of the P2P devices is the P2P Group Owner acting as an “AP” and the other P2P device or devices are 
P2P Clients acting as “client devices.” While inheriting all the latest Wi-Fi technologies including robust security, Wi-Fi 
Direct technology provides the following additional features:  
• P2P discovery to find nearby devices and services   
• Group Owner negotiation to establish a P2P group  
• P2P device power saving and concurrent operation with wireless LAN  
Wi-Fi Alliance launched Wi-Fi Direct certification as a P2P connectivity technology in 2010. Since then, there have been 
significant numbers of certifications. The version of Wi-Fi Direct released in 2010 was based on Wi-Fi 4, WPA2™, and 
Wi-Fi Protected Setup™ technologies with 2.4 GHz and 5 GHz support. In addition, Miracast®, which is used to cast audio 
and video content between client devices, is built upon Wi-Fi Direct.  
To support the adoption of Wi-Fi 6 and WPA3™, Wi-Fi Alliance will release an update to Wi-Fi Direct, which includes the 
latest technologies to improve user experience. This version will make use of the new features that accompany Wi-Fi 6 
and will use WPA3 as its security mechanism.  
Wi-Fi Direct with WPA3 also contains the following advances:   
• Extends the P2P operation to 6 GHz and 5 GHz DFS bands to utilize more spectrum and improve user experience   
• Simplifies P2P discovery using Unsynchronized Service Discovery (USD) and combining two-step discovery 
(device discovery and service discovery) into one step  
• Accelerates P2P connection setup with a secure pairing protocol for WPA3-Personal compliance   
• Optimizes P2P device power saving and provides reliable concurrent operation by using the latest Wi-Fi 
technologies (e.g., target wake time)  
• Supports Bluetooth assisted P2P discovery to reduce the power consumption during the discovery  
• Supports the P2P connection Compatibility mode for backward compatibility with clients that support Wi-Fi Direct 
with WPA2  
 

 
Examples of common use cases for Wi-Fi Direct include:  
• Extended reality (XR) goggles  
• Smartphones  
• Televisions  
• PCs  
• Gaming devices  
• Printers 
About Wi-Fi Alliance®  
Wi-Fi Alliance® is the worldwide network of companies that brings you Wi-Fi®. Members of our collaboration forum come 
together from across the Wi-Fi ecosystem with the shared vision to connect everyone and everything, everywhere, while 
providing the best possible user experience. Since 2000, Wi-Fi Alliance has completed more than 80,000 Wi-Fi 
certifications. The Wi-Fi CERTIFIED® seal of approval designates products with proven interoperability, backward 
compatibility, and the highest industry-standard security protections in place. Today, Wi-Fi carries more than half of the 
internet’s traffic in an ever-expanding variety of applications. Wi-Fi Alliance continues to drive the adoption and evolution 
of Wi-Fi, which billions of people rely on every day.
